content:
Yesterday it was reported that Apple had considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra, before deciding to shelve the plan.

Bloomberg pointed out three reasons behind this decision, one of which is not wanting to clash with the stance Steve Jobs upheld when he launched the original iPhone. However, this is almost certainly not the deciding factor...

A short Apple Pencil designed to work with the iPhone Ultra sounds quite appealing at first glance. The device is essentially an iPhone that can transform into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same functionality is obviously very reasonable.

When Samsung launched the Galaxy Note phablet in 2011, it came with an S-Pen stylus. The idea at the time was that the device could partially replace a paper notebook, and the product continued for a decade with a loyal following before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman listed three reasons why Apple ultimately abandoned the idea:

  • Placing the Pencil on the side of the device instead of the top would make it feel clumsy to hold
  • This would conflict with Steve's view that a stylus is a poor substitute for a finger
  • It would leave unsightly marks on the screen

I don't think the first reason would be the main consideration, as mounting it on the top of the device was also an option. Although this would call for an extremely short design, I think it could still function normally.

I'm similarly not convinced by the second reason. What Steve objected to back then was not the idea that a smartphone could use a stylus, but that the models at the time had to rely on a stylus to operate. Designing the iPhone so that it could be operated nimbly with a finger was the real breakthrough.

In any case, Steve also publicly opposed touch screens on the Mac on the grounds of poor ergonomics, yet we are still expecting the upcoming MacBook Pro models to add touch functionality, which shows that Apple is not averse to overturning positions once held by its co-founder.

I think what really killed the idea is the third reason. The surface of a foldable screen is inevitably thinner and more pliable than that of existing devices. Apple is reportedly said to have waited a long time before launching its first foldable iPhone precisely because of concerns about the screen's appearance and durability; if the Apple Pencil were allowed to repeatedly scrape across the surface, both would be affected.

If Apple ultimately manages to solve this problem, would you like to see an Apple Pencil Mini designed to work with a future iPhone Ultra? Let us know in the comments.
